L195: The carnivorous Venus flytrap catches prey by an ingenious snapping mechanism. Based on work over nearly 200 years, it has become generally accepted that two touches of the trap’s sensory hairs within 30 s, each one generating an action potential, are required to trigger closure of the trap. We developed an electromechanical model, which, however, suggests that under certain circumstances one touch is sufficient to generate two action potentials.
L196: Using a force-sensing microrobotic system, we precisely quantified the sensory-hair deflection parameters necessary to trigger trap closure and correlated them with the elicited action potentials in vivo. Our results confirm the model’s predictions, suggesting that the Venus flytrap may be adapted to a wider range of prey movements than previously assumed.

L207: Abbreviations: AP, action potential; ECB, electromechanical charge buildup; MEMS, microelectromechanical system; RP, receptor potential
L208: ## Introduction
L209: The hunting mechanism of the carnivorous Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula), according to Darwin “the most wonderful plant in the world” [cite70†1 ], has attracted the interest of many scientists, starting with the observations made by Edwards and Nutall, who described the excitability of the sensory hairs but still thought that the capture of insects was accidental [cite71†2 ,cite72†3 ]. Only in the 1830s, Curtis realized that the traps were specifically devoted to catching animal prey [cite73†4 ].
L210: Since then, the individual phases—from trap triggering to reopening after successful digestion—have been investigated from different angles (reviewed in [cite74†5 ]). Starving plants attract insects through the secretion of volatile compounds [cite75†6 ]. While exploring the trap for food, wandering insects accidentally touch one of the six sensory hairs distributed on the two lobes of the trap, thereby triggering an action potential (AP) [cite76†7 –cite77†12 ].
L211: A second touch-triggered AP within about 30 s causes the trap to snap, and the prey is caught. Further APs triggered by the struggling prey induce jasmonic acid biosynthesis and signaling [cite78†13 , cite79†14 ], which seals the trap tightly and eventually leads to the formation of the “green stomach,” a digestive cocktail that mobilizes prey-derived nutrients [cite77†12 , cite80†15 , cite81†16 ].
L212: Here, we focus on the translation of the mechanical stimulation of the sensory hairs into an electrical signal. Although there is a general agreement that sensory-hair deflection opens mechanosensitive ion channels, such channels have not yet been identified [cite82†17 , cite83†18 ]. While these putative channels are open, a receptor potential (RP) builds up [cite84†10 , cite85†19 ], and, if the deflection is large enough, the RP reaches a threshold above which an AP is elicited.
L213: Previous attempts to correlate the mechanical stimuli to the generation of APs suffered from the lack of appropriate instrumentation [cite84†10 , cite85†19 ] and thus were not quantitative, and/or the experiments were done in fixated or dissected, nonfunctional traps [cite86†20 ].
L214: To overcome these shortcomings, we used a microelectromechanical system (MEMS)-based force sensor mounted on a microrobotic system to precisely control the velocity and amplitude of the deflection and to simultaneously measure the applied force in vivo (Figs cite87†1A and 1B and cite88†2 ). In this way, we were able to accurately quantify the parameter range in which hair deflection leads to trap closure, while a second force sensor measured the generated snap force (cite88†Fig 2 ).
L215: In addition, using a noninvasive method, we measured APs to test the deflection conditions under which they are generated.
